paras: The killing of Gray took place in December 1882 in the mountainous part of Hawkins County, Tennessee, when a party of white men came to his cabin at night to whip him over an accusation that he had stolen hogs. In the gunfire that followed, Gray, a Black man, was mortally wounded and died, his stepson's thigh was broken, and two of the white men were wounded. A Knoxville dispatch describing it as a "terrible tragedy" ran in papers across the country.

Gray lived in a cabin in the mountains of Hawkins County, about sixty miles northeast of Knoxville, with his stepson. According to the dispatch, the white men came "for the purpose of whipping him, charging that he had stolen hogs"; the Knoxville Daily Chronicle wrote that Gray "was accused of getting his Christmas pork without paying for it."

The wire account, credited to the Knoxville Tribune, placed the attack on Saturday night, December 23. In that version the men were refused admittance, fired into the cabin, and the fire was returned. Gray was mortally wounded and died soon afterward, and his stepson had a thigh broken by a ball.

Among the attackers, a white man named Jim (or James) Williams was shot in the head and was said to be mortally wounded. A second white man, printed as Arrick, Orrick or Quick in different papers, was also wounded.
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage, and no later report gives Williams's fate.

The story reached most readers through the Knoxville dispatch of December 27, which ran the next day in the Savannah Morning News, the New-York Tribune, the Richmond Dispatch, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, and a day later in Yankton and Burlington papers. Editors headed it "A Tennessee Tragedy," "A Mountain Battle" and "A Dark Record," the last with the subhead "A Deadly Conflict in One of the Dark Places of Tennessee." The New-York Tribune placed it first in a column titled "Deeds of Violence in the South," and the news-in-brief column of The Daily Gazette called the attackers "a gang of white men."

The Knoxville Daily Chronicle treated the affair in a lighter tone, writing that Gray was "not admiring such Christmas festivities" and listing the "Results" in a line. Its brief item still called the wounded white men "assailants," and the Rugby, Tennessee, Rugbeian reprinted the wire wording in its state news column.

The two Knoxville sources disagree on details: the wire put the attack on Saturday night and had the white men fire first, while the Chronicle said Sunday night and that Gray "fired into the crowd of assailants" before they returned fire. Both versions agree that the men had come to whip Gray.

reader.title: Killing of Gray in Hawkins County, Tennessee
bases: A party of white men went at night to a Black man's cabin to whip him over alleged hog theft and an exchange of gunfire followed in which he was killed (A1, A10).

The Knoxville wire crediting the Tribune (A1, A2, A6) and a separate local item in the Knoxville Daily Chronicle (A10), which differs in day and sequence of fire, agree on the core event: white men came to whip Gray, shots were exchanged, Gray was killed and white men were wounded.

accounts.label: Knoxville wire (crediting the Knoxville Tribune)
accounts.gist: White men came Saturday night to whip Gray for alleged hog theft; refused entry, they fired into the cabin and the fire was returned; Gray died, his stepson was wounded, and two white men were wounded.

accounts.label: Knoxville Daily Chronicle
accounts.gist: A party of men tried on Sunday night to whip Gray; Gray fired into them first and they returned fire, killing him and wounding another Black man in the cabin and two white assailants.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Tribune wire as a 'terrible tragedy' and a 'battle', under headlines such as 'A Mountain Battle' and 'A Dark Record'.
The New-York Tribune grouped it with other Southern shootings under 'Deeds of Violence in the South'.
The Knoxville Daily Chronicle wrote it up in a joking tone ('Gray, not admiring such Christmas festivities') while calling the white men 'assailants'.

conflicts.note: Both reports are from Knoxville; neither gives more detail on timing.

info: Saturday night, December 23, 1882, per the wire ('last Saturday night' in Dec. 27 dispatches); the Knoxville Daily Chronicle says Sunday night (Dec. 24).
Gray's cabin, in the mountainous part of Hawkins County, about sixty miles (north)east of Knoxville.
Gray, a Black man ('a negro'), killed; his stepson (the Chronicle says 'another negro in the cabin') wounded, thigh broken by a ball.
Gray was accused of stealing hogs ('getting his Christmas pork without paying for it').
'Some white men', 'a gang of white men', 'a party of men'; unnamed apart from the wounded Jim (James) Williams and a second man named Arrick/Orrick/Quick, whom the Chronicle calls 'white assailants'.
